newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatian stocks closed mixed but outlook said good.
newsitem.headline: Croatian stocks closed mixed but outlook said good.

text.p: Croatian stocks closed mixed in slower trade on Wednesday, with brewery Karlovacka Pivovara leading the gainers, while traders said strong interest was likely to support prices across the board.
"The market continues to be very active and the price movements are very favourable -- I am an optimist," said Josip Ivicic of Consult Invest brokerage.

Karlovacka, a subsidiary of Chile's largest brewery Cervecerias Unidas, was the most actively traded issue with 3,485 shares sold. It ended 25 kuna, or four percent, up at 650. The stock had suffered a slight correction in recent weeks after steady growth from June onwards, but traders said it could now be on the rise again.
"The interest in Karlovacka is still strong, and I expect it to grow further," said Josko Milisa of I.C.F. brokerage.

He said the company's price/earnings ratio of 8.0 was good in comparison with the competition and left room for growth. "Karlovacka could reach the 800-kuna level in the next few months," Milisa said.
Chocolate-maker Kras also traded heavily, selling 451 shares, and ended unchanged from Tuesday at 420 kuna.
Food producer Podravka, which has been constantly rising for the last two weeks, lost 10 kuna to 280 on the day's second-biggest volume of 2,793 shares.
"It is only a correction, Podravka is not going to lose much more," Milisa said. But Ivicic said he expected the food producer to continue losing for another few days.
Market heavyweight drugs firm Pliva added four kuna to close at 599 and trading 318 shares.
Zagrebacka Banka closed 14 kuna down at 2,486 after trading flat for most of the day at 2,500. It sold 1,039 shares.
Another fully listed share, Varazdinska Banka ordinaries, lost 17 kuna to close at 262 on heavy volume of 1,505 shares. Ivicic said he expected the bank to lose a little more before stabilising.
The top gainer, hotelier Suncani Hvar, added three kuna or 5.8 percent to close at 55, selling 259 shares.
Other tourist firms ended mostly flat and traders said they could go up in the autumn on a wave of good publicity following the tourist season.

"There will be a flurry of positive business reports in the newspapers showing that turnover rose between 10 and 30 percent in comparison with 1996," Milisa said. But he predicted hoteliers' significant gains would only materialise in the long run rather than immediately.
Croatia's leading insurer, Croatia Osiguranje, led decliners, losing 210 kuna or 17 percent to 1,000 kuna. But the meagre volume of only 50 shares traded did not allow any conclusions, traders said.
Seven of 18 active issues rose, six fell and five closed flat. Volume shrank to 11,171 from 14,004 units and turnover fell to 7.4 from 16 million kuna.
